facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The Great Kailasa (Cave 16) is attributed to Krishna I (c. 757-83 A.D.), the successor and uncle of Dantidurga.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India attributes the initial commissioning of the Great Kailasa rock-cut complex to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I, whose reign commenced around 757 CE.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: A copper plate grant from Baroda of the period of Karka II (c. 812-13 A.D.) speaks about the greatness of this edifice.
facts.text: The Baroda copper-plate charter of Karkaraja II issued in 812 CE praises a wondrous Shiva temple at Elapura, noting that the chief architect and the gods were astonished by its beauty.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The masons began at the top of the cliff and worked downward, cutting three deep trenches into the rock to isolate a huge U-shaped block.
facts.text: Artisans isolated the core block of the Kailasa temple by excavating 3 massive vertical trenches into the sloping cliffside before chiseling details from top to bottom.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The traditional methods were rigidly followed by the master architect which could not have been achieved by excavating from the front.
facts.text: The subtractive top-to-bottom excavation method allowed stonecutters to work without wooden scaffolding by standing on the living bedrock tiers as they carved downward.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Dhavalikar calculated that about 250 workers cutting 4 cubic feet per day could do the basic excavation work in about five and a half years.
facts.text: Archaeologist M. K. Dhavalikar calculated that a crew of 250 stonecutters removing 4 cubic feet of basalt per day could have finished the primary rough quarrying phase within 5.5 years.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: It is estimated that the artists removed 3,000,000 cu ft (85,000 m3) of stone, weighing approximately 200,000 t (220,000 tons), to excavate the temple.
facts.text: While popular literature widely cites that roughly 200,000 tonnes of basalt were quarried to create Cave 16, modern architectural estimates dispute this exact figure and place the excavated mass between 150,000 and 400,000 tonnes based on differing courtyard boundary assumptions.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: M. K. Dhavalikar (1982) analyzed the architecture of the temple, and concluded that the major part of the temple was completed during the reign of Krishna I, although he agreed with Goetz that some other parts of the temple complex can be dated to the later rulers.
facts.text: While Hermann Goetz argued that the Kailasa complex was sculpted in distinct phases over multiple centuries across different dynasties, M. K. Dhavalikar argued that the core architectural scheme was planned and executed primarily during Krishna I's single reign with only minor later additions.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Dhavalikar dated the famous sculpture of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa to about three or four decades after the main temple, attributing it to later Rashtrakuta patronage.
facts.text: While some art historians regard the monumental relief of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa as part of the original 8th-century design, M. K. Dhavalikar dated the sculpture to approximately 40 years after Krishna I's death based on changing stylistic idioms.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: According to this legend, the local king suffered from a severe disease. His queen prayed to the god Ghrishneshwar (Shiva) at Elapura to cure her husband. She vowed to construct a temple if her wish was granted, and promised to observe a fast until she could see the shikhara (top) of this temple.
facts.text: The 16th-century Marathi text Katha-Kalpataru by Krishna Yajnavalki records that Queen Manikavati vowed to observe an unbroken fast until she could see the shikhara of the proposed temple at Elapura.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Kokasa assured the king that the queen would be able to see the shikhara within a week. He started carving the temple from the top, by excavating downwards.
facts.text: The Katha-Kalpataru text relates that an architect named Kokasa resolved the queen's crisis by beginning carving at the mountain top, thereby making the temple spire visible within 1 week.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to historians, the temple was built in 18 years using the most basic tools, such as hammers and chisels.
facts.text: A pervasive modern folk belief claims that the entire Kailasa temple complex was miraculously carved from the mountain in exactly 18 years using only rudimentary iron chisels and hammers.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: A local legend claims that the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb attempted to destroy the Kailasa temple, but failed, causing only minor damages.
facts.text: A popular regional legend alleges that the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb dispatched over 1,000 workers to destroy the Kailasa temple over 3 full years, but they could only disfigure a handful of statues before giving up.
